lesson.title: The Rhythm Breaks: Understanding Jitter in Real Time Traffic
lesson.summary: Jitter measures how much packet delay varies from one packet to the next, and it is what makes voice and video calls sound choppy even when average latency looks fine.
lesson.body:
Jitter is the variation in delay from one packet to the next, rather than the delay itself. Two packets sent along the same path a moment apart can take noticeably different amounts of time to arrive, and jitter measures how much that timing bounces around instead of staying constant. A network can have relatively low average latency and still have high jitter, or the reverse, so jitter is tracked as its own separate metric alongside latency and RTT.

The dominant cause of jitter is the queuing delay covered earlier in this chapter sequence. Propagation delay and transmission delay for a given packet size and link are essentially fixed, but queuing delay changes from moment to moment depending on how much other traffic is competing for the same router buffers. When traffic is light, a packet might sail through a router with almost no wait. Moments later, if a burst of other traffic arrives first, a similar packet on the same path might sit in a queue for several extra milliseconds. That difference from packet to packet is exactly what jitter captures.

Consider five packets sent one after another, with one way delays of 20, 22, 45, 21, and 23 milliseconds. A simple way to see the jitter is to look at the differences between consecutive packets: 2, 23, 24, and 2 milliseconds. Averaging those differences gives about 12.75 milliseconds of jitter, driven almost entirely by that one packet that took 45 milliseconds instead of the roughly 20 milliseconds the others took, most likely because it hit a router at a moment of heavier queuing.

Jitter matters most for real time applications like voice calls, video conferencing, and online gaming, where packets need to be played back or acted on at a steady pace. A voice call can tolerate a consistent 150 milliseconds of one way delay reasonably well, because both sides adapt to a steady rhythm, but wildly varying delay causes audio to arrive in uneven bursts, producing choppy or garbled sound even if the average delay is fine. Applications handle this with a jitter buffer, a small amount of intentional extra delay added at the receiving end that holds packets briefly and releases them at a steady rate, smoothing out the underlying variation at the cost of a little additional latency.

Real time transport protocols formalize this idea. RTP, the protocol most voice and video applications use to carry media over the network, has receivers maintain a running smoothed estimate of interarrival jitter as calls progress, which applications can use to size their jitter buffers dynamically rather than guessing a fixed value in advance.

Jitter ties directly back to everything covered so far: it is built from the same delay components as latency and RTT, but it isolates the part of those delays that is unpredictable, which in practice almost always traces back to variable queuing delay rather than the comparatively stable transmission and propagation delay terms.
